sessions.title: Random experiments, outcomes, sample spaces & events
sessions.focus: Finite experiments, atomic outcomes and event subsets.
sessions.purpose: Create the probability objects before assigning numbers.
sessions.centralCapability: Model an uncertainty experiment with a finite sample space and events.
sessions.principalObstacle: Events are confused with single outcomes or verbal labels are left without an explicit sample space.
requiredOwnership: Define the experiment and atomic outcomes.
Construct a complete finite sample space.
Represent an event as a subset of the sample space.
Distinguish an outcome from an event.
Form event intersection/union from stated conditions.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Model an unfamiliar finite experiment and translate verbal conditions into event subsets.
sessions.lesson: A random experiment has an uncertain result; an outcome is one atomic result, the sample space Ω lists all possible atomic outcomes, and an event is any subset of Ω. Compound experiments often use ordered tuples, so order must be preserved when it matters. Worked example: A spinner labelled R,G,B is spun once. Ω={R,G,B}. Event C='not blue' is {R,G}; R is one outcome, whereas {R,G} is an event. If a second spinner labelled 1,2 is added, outcomes are ordered pairs such as (G,2). Guided check: A coin is tossed and then a digit from {1,2,3} is chosen. Write Ω and the event 'tail and an odd digit'.

sessions.title: Finite probability models, axioms & normalization
sessions.focus: Assigning legal weights to finite outcomes.
sessions.purpose: Separate sample-space structure from probability weights.
sessions.centralCapability: Validate and complete a finite probability model using nonnegativity and total mass 1.
sessions.principalObstacle: Probability is treated as automatically uniform or weights are accepted without normalization.
requiredOwnership: Assign probability to atomic outcomes.
Check nonnegativity.
Check total probability equals 1.
Solve a missing probability by normalization.
Compute an event probability by summing atomic weights.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Audit or complete a nonuniform finite model and calculate event probabilities.
sessions.lesson: A finite probability model assigns each atomic outcome ω a weight P({ω})≥0 and all atomic weights sum to 1. An event probability is the sum of the weights of the outcomes inside it; equal weights are a special case, not the definition. Worked example: For Ω={a,b,c}, weights 0.2,0.5,0.3 are legal because all are nonnegative and sum to1. If E={a,c}, then P(E)=0.2+0.3=0.5. Guided check: On Ω={u,v,w,x}, weights are 0.1,0.25,0.4,p. Find p and P({v,x}).

sessions.title: Equally likely outcomes & counting probability
sessions.focus: Favourable-over-total counts when atomic outcomes truly have equal probability.
sessions.purpose: Connect M03 counting to finite probability without assuming uniformity by default.
sessions.centralCapability: Use counting only after justifying equal atomic probabilities.
sessions.principalObstacle: Favourable/total is used in nonuniform spaces or the denominator counts the wrong atomic outcomes.
requiredOwnership: Justify when atomic outcomes are equally likely.
Count the total atomic outcomes.
Count favourable outcomes.
Compute favourable/total probability.
Reject favourable/total when equiprobability is absent.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve a counting probability and state why the denominator is legitimate.
sessions.lesson: If every atomic outcome in Ω has the same probability, then P(E)=|E|/|Ω|. The formula comes from equal weights 1/|Ω|; it is invalid when atomic outcomes have unequal weights. Worked example: Choose one ordered pair from {1,2,3}×{A,B} uniformly. There are6 equally likely pairs. Event 'number is 2 or 3 and letter B' has2 favourable pairs, so probability2/6=1/3. Guided check: A 4-character code is chosen uniformly from {0,1}^4. Count the codes with exactly one 1 and compute the probability.

sessions.title: Complements, certainty, impossibility & at-least-one basics
sessions.focus: Complement rule and boundary events.
sessions.purpose: Make complement reasoning automatic before harder repeated-trial problems.
sessions.centralCapability: Use P(A^c)=1−P(A) and identify certain/impossible events.
sessions.principalObstacle: Complement is confused with 'opposite-looking' wording or at-least-one is counted directly when none is easier.
requiredOwnership: Identify event complement exactly.
Use P(A^c)=1−P(A).
Recognize P(Ω)=1.
Recognize P(∅)=0.
Use a complement to compute an at-least-one event in a finite model.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Translate verbal complements exactly and use them to simplify probability calculations.
sessions.lesson: The complement A^c contains exactly the outcomes not in A, so A and A^c partition Ω and P(A^c)=1−P(A). Therefore P(Ω)=1 and P(∅)=0. 'At least one' is often the complement of 'none.' Worked example: A uniform 8-sided spinner is labelled1–8. Event A='multiple of3' is {3,6}; A^c has six outcomes, so P(A^c)=6/8=3/4=1−1/4. Guided check: Three equally likely binary answers are generated independently only as a sample-space listing exercise. Using the 8 equally likely strings, find the probability of at least one 1 by complementing the single string 000.

sessions.title: Union, intersection & the addition rule
sessions.focus: Disjoint and overlapping event combinations.
sessions.purpose: Translate event algebra into probability arithmetic.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute unions/intersections and apply the disjoint addition rule with correct conditions.
sessions.principalObstacle: Probabilities are added blindly even when events overlap.
requiredOwnership: Interpret A∪B and A∩B as events.
Identify whether two events are disjoint.
Use P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B) for disjoint events.
Explain why overlap causes double counting.
Compute simple union/intersection probabilities from an explicit finite model.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Decide whether addition is legal and compute event combinations from a finite model.
sessions.lesson: A∪B means A or B (inclusive), while A∩B means both. If A∩B=∅, the events are disjoint and P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B). If they overlap, direct addition counts the overlap twice. Worked example: On a uniform die, A={1,2} and B={5,6} are disjoint, so P(A∪B)=2/6+2/6=4/6. If C={2,3}, A and C overlap at2, so direct addition would double-count that outcome. Guided check: On a uniform 10-outcome space, E has3 outcomes, F has4 and they are disjoint. Compute P(E∪F), then state what extra information is needed if they overlap.

sessions.title: Two-event inclusion–exclusion in probability
sessions.focus: Correcting overlap in union probabilities.
sessions.purpose: Generalize the addition rule to arbitrary two events.
sessions.centralCapability: Use and justify P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).
sessions.principalObstacle: Intersection is subtracted with the wrong sign or omitted.
requiredOwnership: State the two-event inclusion-exclusion formula.
Explain the overlap correction.
Solve for a union probability.
Rearrange the formula to recover an intersection.
Check probability bounds/consistency.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Use inclusion-exclusion forward and backward and detect inconsistent inputs.
sessions.lesson: Because A∩B is included once in P(A) and once in P(B), adding the two probabilities counts it twice. Subtracting P(A∩B) once gives P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). Worked example: If P(A)=0.45,P(B)=0.35 and P(A∩B)=0.15, then P(A∪B)=0.45+0.35−0.15=0.65. The answer cannot exceed1. Guided check: If P(E∪F)=0.7,P(E)=0.4,P(F)=0.5, solve for P(E∩F).

sessions.title: Conditional probability as a restricted universe
sessions.focus: P(A|B) and denominator discipline.
sessions.purpose: Make conditioning a change of reference population rather than a formula trick.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute and interpret P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) when P(B)>0.
sessions.principalObstacle: The denominator remains the original sample space or conditioning on probability-zero events is ignored.
requiredOwnership: Interpret conditioning as restricting to B.
Use P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B).
Use the correct denominator P(B).
Distinguish P(A|B) from P(B|A).
State the P(B)>0 requirement.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute and explain a conditional probability with the right restricted universe and zero-denominator caveat.
sessions.lesson: Conditioning on B means we now reason only among outcomes in B and renormalize their probability to1. For P(B)>0, P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B). Reversing the bar changes the denominator and usually changes the value. Worked example: A uniform card numbered1–10 is chosen. Given that it is even (five possibilities), the chance it is above6 is2/5 because the restricted universe is {2,4,6,8,10}. Guided check: On a uniform die, compute P(result is even | result>2) by listing the restricted outcomes first.

sessions.title: Multiplication rule & intersections from conditionals
sessions.focus: Turning conditional probabilities into joint probabilities.
sessions.purpose: Connect restricted-universe reasoning to sequential/joint events.
sessions.centralCapability: Use P(A∩B)=P(B)P(A|B)=P(A)P(B|A).
sessions.principalObstacle: Conditional and joint probabilities are multiplied or compared without tracking which event is the conditioning base.
requiredOwnership: State the multiplication rule.
Compute an intersection from a conditional probability.
Use either ordering consistently.
Recover a conditional from a joint probability.
Check that a joint probability cannot exceed either marginal.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Move correctly between joint and conditional probabilities.
sessions.lesson: Rearranging the conditional-probability definition gives P(A∩B)=P(B)P(A|B). The same intersection can also be written P(A)P(B|A). A joint probability cannot exceed either marginal because A∩B is a subset of each. Worked example: If P(B)=0.40 and P(A|B)=0.25, then P(A∩B)=0.10. If P(A)=0.50, this also implies P(B|A)=0.10/0.50=0.20. Guided check: Given P(C)=0.6 and P(D|C)=0.3, find P(C∩D), then compare the result with P(C).

sessions.title: Probability trees & multi-stage paths
sessions.focus: Branch probabilities, path products and disjoint leaf sums.
sessions.purpose: Make multi-stage finite processes visible and auditable.
sessions.centralCapability: Build a probability tree, multiply along paths and add disjoint leaves.
sessions.principalObstacle: Branch probabilities are added along a path or conditional labels are treated as unconditional.
requiredOwnership: Construct a correctly labelled two-stage tree.
Ensure outgoing branch probabilities sum to1.
Multiply conditional probabilities along a path.
Add disjoint leaf probabilities for an event.
Check all leaf probabilities sum to1.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Model and solve a two-stage finite process with a probability tree.
sessions.lesson: At each node, outgoing conditional branch probabilities sum to1. A leaf probability is the product along its path; an event covering several leaves is the sum of those disjoint leaf probabilities. All leaf probabilities together must sum to1. Worked example: Stage1 chooses L with0.6 or R with0.4. Given L, success has0.5; given R, success has0.25. Leaf probabilities are .30,.30,.10,.30 and sum1; total success=.30+.10=.40. Guided check: A process chooses A with0.7 or B with0.3; conditional pass probabilities are0.8 and0.4. Write the four leaf probabilities.

sessions.title: Sampling with vs without replacement
sessions.focus: How sampling protocol changes later conditional probabilities.
sessions.purpose: Prevent independence assumptions from being smuggled into sequential draws.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute sequential probabilities under replacement and without replacement.
sessions.principalObstacle: The second-draw denominator/composition is left unchanged even when the first draw removes an item.
requiredOwnership: State how replacement changes the state.
Compute an ordered two-draw probability with replacement.
Compute it without replacement.
Update numerator and denominator after a draw.
Compare the resulting dependence structures qualitatively.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve and compare replacement/nonreplacement sampling problems.
sessions.lesson: With replacement, the population composition resets before the next draw; without replacement, both the total and possibly the category count change. That state change alters the next conditional probability. Worked example: A bag has3 red and2 blue balls. P(red then blue) with replacement=(3/5)(2/5)=6/25. Without replacement=(3/5)(2/4)=3/10. Guided check: From a box with4 good and1 bad item, compare P(good then good) with and without replacement.

sessions.title: Independence via the product rule
sessions.focus: Event independence as factorization of joint probability.
sessions.purpose: Replace vague 'unrelated' intuition with a testable definition.
sessions.centralCapability: Test A and B using P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).
sessions.principalObstacle: Events are called independent because they look separate or occur in different descriptions.
requiredOwnership: State the product definition of independence.
Compute both sides of the independence test.
Conclude independence or dependence from equality/inequality.
Distinguish definition from causal intuition.
Use product factorization to recompute a joint probability after independence is established.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Test independence numerically and use it only when justified.
sessions.lesson: Events A and B are independent when P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). This is a probability statement, not a claim that one event physically causes nothing about the other. Once independence is established or given, the same factorization can be used to compute the joint. Worked example: Roll a fair die twice. A='first roll is even' and B='second roll is6'. P(A)=1/2,P(B)=1/6 and P(A∩B)=3/36=1/12=(1/2)(1/6), so they are independent; the factorization then reproduces the same joint. Guided check: On a uniform die, test A={1,2,3} and B={1,4} using the product criterion.

sessions.title: Independence via conditioning; diagnosing dependence
sessions.focus: P(A|B)=P(A) when P(B)>0.
sessions.purpose: Connect product and conditional definitions and expose dependence as probability change.
sessions.centralCapability: Test whether conditioning changes an event probability.
sessions.principalObstacle: A changed conditional probability is overlooked or conditional equality is used when P(B)=0.
requiredOwnership: State the conditional criterion for independence when P(B)>0.
Compare P(A|B) with P(A).
Diagnose dependence from a change.
Relate the conditional criterion to the product rule.
Respect the positive-denominator condition.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Diagnose dependence from conditioning and connect both definitions.
sessions.lesson: For P(B)>0, A and B are independent exactly when P(A|B)=P(A). If conditioning on B changes A's probability, they are dependent. The unconditional probability can be obtained from the disjoint first-stage branches already owned from probability trees. Worked example: From a bag with2 red and2 blue, draw two without replacement. P(second red)=(2/4)(1/3)+(2/4)(2/3)=1/2, while P(second red | first red)=1/3, so the draw-colour events are dependent. Guided check: With replacement from the same bag, compute P(second red) from the two first-draw branches and compare it with P(second red | first red).

sessions.title: Mutual exclusivity vs independence
sessions.focus: Disjoint events are usually dependent, not independent.
sessions.purpose: Eliminate one of the most common probability category errors.
sessions.centralCapability: Contrast A∩B=∅ with P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).
sessions.principalObstacle: 'Cannot happen together' is mistaken for 'do not affect each other'.
requiredOwnership: Define mutual exclusivity/disjointness.
Define independence.
Show positive-probability disjoint events cannot be independent.
Handle the zero-probability edge case.
Give or diagnose examples of each relationship.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Classify event pairs without conflating structural disjointness and probabilistic independence.
sessions.lesson: Mutually exclusive events satisfy A∩B=∅. Independent events satisfy P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). If both events have positive probability and are disjoint, then0=P(A∩B)<P(A)P(B), so they cannot be independent. A zero-probability event is the edge case. Worked example: On a fair die, A={1,2},B={5,6} are disjoint with probabilities1/3 each. Their joint is0 but product1/9, so they are not independent. Guided check: Explain why ∅ is disjoint from every event and also independent of every event under the product definition.

sessions.title: Pairwise vs mutual independence
sessions.focus: Three-event independence and hidden higher-order dependence.
sessions.purpose: Prevent pairwise checks from being overgeneralized.
sessions.centralCapability: Distinguish pairwise factorization from full three-event factorization.
sessions.principalObstacle: Checking all three pairs is assumed to prove mutual independence.
requiredOwnership: Define pairwise independence for three events.
State the additional triple condition for mutual independence.
Verify all pairwise products.
Check the triple intersection.
Construct/diagnose a pairwise-but-not-mutually-independent example.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Audit a three-event independence claim at pair and triple levels.
sessions.lesson: For three events A,B,C, pairwise independence means each of the three pairs factors. Mutual independence requires those pairwise conditions and also P(A∩B∩C)=P(A)P(B)P(C). Pairwise checks alone therefore do not logically settle the triple. Worked example: Toss three fair coins independently and let A,B,C mean heads on toss1,toss2,toss3. Each marginal is1/2, every pair intersection is1/4, and the triple intersection is1/8, so the three events are mutually independent. As a contrasting ordinary dependence example on one fair die, E='even' and F='>3' have joint2/6 while P(E)P(F)=1/4, so even the pair condition fails. Guided check: State exactly which four factorization checks are needed to establish mutual independence of three events.

sessions.title: Repeated independent trials & ordered success/failure paths
sessions.focus: Probability of one exact ordered pattern.
sessions.purpose: Prepare exact-k counting without prematurely invoking a named distribution.
sessions.centralCapability: Multiply p and 1−p across an exact independent sequence.
sessions.principalObstacle: Order is ignored too early or trial independence is assumed without being stated.
requiredOwnership: Identify repeated identical independent trials.
Assign success probability p and failure1−p.
Compute an exact ordered path probability.
Count powers by number of successes/failures.
Explain why a different ordering has the same probability when p is constant.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
inScope: Repeated Bernoulli-style finite trials without distribution naming
sessions.exitCondition: Compute exact ordered success/failure path probabilities and justify the multiplication.
sessions.lesson: For independent repeated trials with constant success probability p, an exact path with s successes and f failures has probability p^s(1−p)^f. The order changes the path identity but not its probability when every trial uses the same p. Worked example: A shot succeeds independently with p=0.6. The exact path S,F,S has probability .6·.4·.6=.144. F,S,S has the same .144 because it has two successes and one failure. Guided check: With independent success probability0.7, compute the probability of S,S,F,F.

sessions.title: Exactly-k successes via combinations
sessions.focus: Counting all ordered paths with k successes.
sessions.purpose: Derive the familiar exactly-k finite-trial formula from M03 combinations plus M04 path probabilities.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k) without treating it as a memorized distribution formula.
sessions.principalObstacle: The path probability is computed but the number of placements is omitted or multiplied twice.
requiredOwnership: Count success-position choices with C(n,k).
Compute one path probability p^k(1−p)^(n−k).
Multiply count by path probability.
Explain why the paths are disjoint and equally probable.
Avoid naming/using unintroduced distribution machinery.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Derive and apply exactly-k success probability from first principles.
sessions.lesson: Exactly k successes in n independent constant-p trials is a disjoint union of C(n,k) ordered paths. Each such path has probability p^k(1−p)^(n−k), so the total is their count times one path probability. Worked example: Four independent trials with p=1/2 have exactly two successes in C(4,2)=6 paths. Each path has probability(1/2)^4=1/16, so total6/16=3/8. Guided check: For n=3,p=0.4, derive the probability of exactly one success by counting its three possible positions.

sessions.focus: Repeated-trial complements.
sessions.purpose: Make 'at least one' calculations efficient and transparent.
sessions.centralCapability: Use P(at least one)=1−P(none) under independent repeated trials.
sessions.principalObstacle: Many overlapping cases are added directly or independence is omitted when computing none/all.
requiredOwnership: Translate at-least-one to the complement of none.
Compute none under independence.
Compute all under independence.
Use the complement rule to get at least one.
Compare direct case counting versus complement efficiency.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Choose the complement route for none/at-least-one/all events and justify each factor.
sessions.lesson: For n independent trials with success probability p, 'none succeed' has probability(1−p)^n, so 'at least one succeeds'=1−(1−p)^n. 'All succeed'=p^n. The complement often replaces many overlapping cases with one exact path. Worked example: Three independent alarms trigger with probability0.1 each. None trigger=.9^3=.729, so at least one triggers=.271; all trigger=.001. Guided check: Four independent messages are delivered with p=.8. Compute none, at least one and all.

sessions.title: Partitions & the law of total probability
sessions.focus: Forward probability through mutually exclusive exhaustive cases.
sessions.purpose: Provide the denominator engine Bayes will later invert without teaching Bayes early.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute P(A)=ΣP(B_i)P(A|B_i) over a finite partition.
sessions.principalObstacle: Case weights are omitted, partition branches overlap, or posterior probabilities are computed prematurely.
requiredOwnership: Identify a finite partition.
Verify partition events are disjoint and exhaustive.
Compute branch joint probabilities.
Sum branch contributions to a target event.
State the finite law of total probability without posterior inversion.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute a forward marginal probability by partitioning the sample space.
sessions.lesson: If B1,…,Bk are disjoint and cover Ω, then A is split into disjoint pieces A∩Bi. Therefore P(A)=ΣP(Bi)P(A|Bi). This is a forward marginalization rule; solving backward for P(Bi|A) is Bayes territory and comes later. Worked example: A job comes from source1 with.7 or source2 with.3. Error probabilities are.02 and.05. Total error=.7·.02+.3·.05=.029. Guided check: A customer is weekday with.8 or weekend with.2; purchase rates are.1 and.25. Compute the overall purchase probability only.

sessions.purpose: Introduce expectation before decision theory or formal random-variable distributions.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute E[X]=Σx(ω)P(ω) for a finite numerical function/payoff.
sessions.principalObstacle: Expected value is confused with probability, guaranteed payoff or the most likely payoff.
requiredOwnership: Associate a numerical payoff/value with each outcome.

sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.

sessions.lesson: For a finite outcome model with numerical value X(ω), the expectation is E[X]=Σω X(ω)P(ω). It is a probability-weighted average. It may be a value that never occurs and is not a guarantee. Worked example: Outcomes pay −2,1,5 with probabilities .25,.5,.25. E=−.5+.5+1.25=1.25, even though1.25 is not an available payoff. Guided check: Values0,4,10 occur with probabilities.5,.3,.2. Verify normalization and compute the weighted average.

sessions.focus: Arithmetic mean of values under uniform atomic probability.
sessions.purpose: Connect uniform probability and symmetry to efficient expectation calculation.
sessions.centralCapability: Use equal weights to average values and exploit balanced pairing when justified.
sessions.principalObstacle: The arithmetic mean is used even when outcomes are not equally likely.
requiredOwnership: Recognize when expectation reduces to an arithmetic mean.
Compute the mean over equally likely atomic outcomes.
Use symmetry/pairing to simplify a finite mean.
Explain why repeated value labels still need atomic multiplicity.

sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute uniform finite expectation efficiently and know when simple averaging is invalid.
sessions.lesson: If N atomic outcomes are equally likely, E[X]=(1/N)ΣX(ω). Pair1 with6,2 with5,3 with4; every pair averages3.5, so the overall expectation is3.5. Guided check: A uniform choice from {2,6,10,14} has what expectation? Use pairing rather than summing first.

sessions.lesson: On one finite sample space, E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c because finite sums distribute over addition and constants. No independence assumption appears. Linearity concerns sums and scalar multiples; it does not say nonlinear operations commute with expectation. Worked example: On two equally likely outcomes, X=(0,2) and Y=(1,3). E[X]=1,E[Y]=2. Directly, 2X−Y+5 has values4,6, mean5; linearity gives2·1−2+5=5. But E[X²]=(0+4)/2=2, while(E[X])²=1, so squaring is not linear. Guided check: If E[X]=3 and E[Y]=−1, compute E[4X+2Y−7] and state whether independence is needed.

sessions.lesson: For event A, the indicator I_A is1 when A occurs and0 otherwise, so E[I_A]=1·P(A)+0·P(A^c)=P(A). If N=I1+⋯+Ik counts occurrences, linearity gives E[N]=ΣP(event_i), even when the indicators are dependent. Worked example: Draw two balls without replacement from a bag with3 red and2 blue. Let I1,I2 indicate red on each draw. By symmetry P(red on each position)=3/5, so E[number red]=E[I1]+E[I2]=6/5, despite dependence between draws. Guided check: Choose a 2-person committee uniformly from4 people, two of whom are labelled A-type. Define indicators for each A-type person being selected and compute the expected number selected.

sessions.exitCondition: Interpret an expectation without overclaiming what it predicts or recommends.
sessions.lesson: Expectation is one probability-weighted average. It need not be the most likely outcome, need not be attainable, and is never a guarantee. Two payoff models can share an expectation while differing radically in spread; choosing between them requires decision criteria that M05 will introduce. Worked example: Model A pays0 with.5 or10 with.5, so E=5; model B pays5 for sure, also E=5. The same expectation does not make the outcome patterns identical. Guided check: A payoff is1 with.9 and31 with.1. Compute expectation and identify the most likely payoff.

sessions.lesson: Synthesis begins by naming the partition, events and numerical values before calculating. Use path multiplication for leaves, total probability for a forward marginal, compare conditional and marginal probabilities for independence, then take a probability-weighted average if a numerical value is supplied. Do not reverse conditionals unless the task explicitly enters M06. Worked example: A shipment comes from North with probability0.2 or South with0.8. Conditional on North, damage probability is0.10; conditional on South it is0.30. The damage leaves are.02 and.24, so total damage=.26. Since P(damage|North)=.10 differs from.26, source and damage are dependent. If damage has value−5 and no-damage value1, expected value is(−5)(.26)+1(.74)=−.56. Guided check: A device is mode L with.3 or R with.7; conditional alarm rates are.2 and.4. Compute total alarm and say whether mode and alarm are independent.
